evidence.finding: Mean AHT increased 39.7%, from 375.2 seconds before the incident to 524.2 seconds incident-and-after.
At 09:15, AHT jumped from 368.2 to 458.3 seconds while service level fell from 85.1% to 75.3%; service level subsequently averaged 60.4%.
Mean ASA increased from 30.6 to 65.3 seconds, while answered calls fell 17.2% despite stable offered demand.
Scheduled and logged-in staffing remained at 49; productive staffing changed only from 45.4 to 45.27 agents.
AHT increased by approximately 40% to 41% in all four queues, with unchanged queue staffing.
Account Support volume increased 16.3%, amplifying that queue's degradation but not explaining the center-wide incident.
No mismatch was found: recalculated service level matched every reported interval exactly, with a maximum difference of 0.0 percentage points.

primary_root_cause_detail: A broad, sustained increase in average handle time reduced throughput against essentially unchanged staffing and demand. AHT rose at the 09:15 incident boundary and increased by about 40% across every visible queue. The visible data does not identify the underlying process reason for the longer interactions.
recommended_actions: Identify the interaction or after-call-work components that increased at 09:15 across all queues, segmented by contact reason and agent workflow.
Review process, script, knowledge-base, or system changes capable of increasing handle time across every queue.
Apply temporary capacity or workload controls until AHT returns to baseline, prioritizing Account Support because of its localized volume increase and larger service-level decline.
Monitor interval-level AHT, occupancy, answered throughput, ASA, and service level to verify recovery.

rejected_hypotheses.reason: Center offered volume averaged 2.6% lower after onset; only Account Support had a moderate localized increase.
Scheduled and logged-in headcount remained constant, and productive staffing declined only 0.28%.
All queues showed nearly identical proportional AHT growth, and no visible event corroborated a routing change.
No visible platform event corroborated an incident during the evaluation window.
Service level recalculated exactly from visible counts in all 16 intervals.

stakeholder_summary: The service-level incident was most likely caused by a center-wide increase in handle time, not by a demand surge or staffing loss. AHT rose about 40% at the incident onset across all queues, consuming available capacity and reducing throughput. Account Support's moderate volume increase worsened its local impact. The operational reason for the AHT increase requires follow-up.
